item.title: [World news | The Guardian] The return of the caspian tiger: how a species feared extinct has come back to Kazakhstan
item.description:
The wild capture and release of a female big cat into a nature reserve is the first step towards reintroducing a population that hasn’t been seen for 70 years

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.

Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt's inclusion in Mecca agreement, sources say
item.description:
Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt's inclusion in Mecca agreement, sources say

Submitted by Faisal Edroos on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 18:00
The kingdom didn't want Egypt to join the new defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan despite Ankara's push for Cairo to be included, sources say
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan (L), Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (C), and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif pose after signing a joint defence agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Turkish presidential press office/Handout via Reuters)
Off

Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed with Turkey and Pakistan last week, despite Ankara's push for Cairo to be included in the pact, three Saudi sources familiar with the discussions told Middle East Eye.

One of the sources, a former senior adviser to the Saudi monarchy, said Riyadh did not want Egypt to join the agreement "at least for now".

All three sources, however, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the issue, said the Saudi position was driven by a growing frustration with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's government and a belief in Riyadh that Egypt no longer offered the strategic or military value it once did.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which was signed in the Holy Muslim city of Mecca on Friday, commits Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to regard an armed attack against any one of the three countries as an attack against all three. 

Saudi officials have described it as a mechanism to strengthen joint defence capabilities, despite the agreement being vague on operational mechanisms, specific triggers, and how joint military assistance would actually be executed in a crisis. 

According to the sources, the Saudi decision to oppose Egypt's entry was due to simmering tensions between Riyadh and Cairo.

They said that Saudi Arabia was the biggest financial supporter of Sisi's government after he seized power in a 2013 coup, initially spending around $25b to shore up Cairo's flagging economy, but Riyadh had become frustrated by what it regards as a lack of reciprocal support on key security issues.

One of the sources pointed to Egypt's "minimal and unreliable" role in Saudi Arabia's lengthy war with Yemen's Houthis and its let-down position during the US and Israeli war on Iran.

They also cited growing unease over Cairo's "subordination" to the United Arab Emirates, specifically after the fallout between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi over the latter's support for Southern Yemeni separatist groups that "threaten Saudi's national security and interests".

'Egypt has always been a dependent on us, on the US, and it does not give back, it just takes and takes with no return'

- Former senior adviser to the Saudi monarchy

Two of the sources noted that while Egypt sent fighter jets to Abu Dhabi in response to the Iranian attacks, and Sisi was keen to visit UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed more than once during the war, no such steps were taken towards Saudi Arabia. They concluded that Riyadh had become increasingly alarmed by Sisi's alignment with Abu Dhabi.

The sources said this was due to Riyadh seeing several Emirati policies as running against Egypt's own strategic interests. These include the UAE’s involvement in Somaliland, its strategic relationship with Israel, its support for Ethiopia during disputes over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and its backing of the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan.

One of the sources said that Cairo's continued engagement with Abu Dhabi had deepened doubts in Riyadh about Egypt's reliability as a strategic partner.

Another source described the relationship under Sisi as increasingly one in which Saudi Arabia sees Egypt as "dependent" on Gulf support rather than as a reliable partner.

The former senior adviser said Egypt had historically been dependent on the kingdom, the United States and other outside powers while providing little in return.

"Egypt has always been a dependent on us, on the US, and it does not give back, it just takes and takes with no return," the adviser said.

Turkey wanted Egypt in the pact

On Saturday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan suggested that Cairo was a "natural partner" for Ankara and that there was no reason it could not eventually become part of the alliance once technical issues were resolved.

Several Turkish sources subsequently told MEE that Ankara had made considerable efforts to include Egypt in the treaty and had formally proposed its participation.

However, once it became clear that Cairo was not prepared to join, the other countries decided to proceed without it, according to the Turkish sources.

The Saudi sources, however, disputed the suggestion that Egypt itself had rejected the pact.

The former senior adviser, who is still close to the country's decision-making, described it as “laughable” to suggest Cairo had decided not to participate.

"The matter of fact is, Sisi would have been eager to join so he can reap the financial gains of this agreement, as he usually does," the adviser said.

The adviser said Saudi decision-makers had serious concerns about Sisi’s loyalty and did not believe he could be trusted in the same way as the Turkish and Pakistani leaderships.

"We understand that the Turks wanted Egypt to be included, and understand why," the adviser said. "Maybe in the future, if we see that there is change or improvement."

But the Saudi sources said Turkey and Pakistan offered more to the alliance militarily than Egypt.

Turkey has an increasingly sophisticated defence industry, while Pakistan has an established weapons manufacturing sector and a large standing military.

In contrast, the sources said Egypt's military manufacturing capacity is concentrated heavily on civilian production and does not offer the same level of advanced defence technology.

"The role of the military should be to invest in its military manufacturing capabilities, rather than busy itself in investing and managing food factories," one of the sources said.

They also questioned the combat readiness and effectiveness of the Egyptian armed forces.

The sources said the decision was therefore not simply about Egypt’s political alignment but about what Riyadh believes Cairo could tangibly contribute to a new regional security architecture.

Egypt's diminishing role

The Saudi assessment comes amid a broader debate over Egypt's diminishing role in the region.

The Economist reported on Monday that Egypt, which had long presented itself as a pillar of the regional order, had been "sidelined as a mediator and military power".

For decades, Egypt was a central military partner for Gulf states, including during the US-led coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991. In contrast to now, where the sources pointed out that Kuwait is now more keen to join the Makkah agreement rather than having the military alliance it once had with Egypt for its protection. 

But the Saudi sources argued that under Sisi, Egypt had become increasingly dependent on outside financial support while offering less in return on major regional security issues.

The former senior adviser said the kingdom regarded its relationships with Ankara, despite being turbulent in recent years, as being more reliable than its relationship with Cairo.

"The decision makers in the leadership have serious concerns about Sisi's loyalty," the adviser said. 

"He is simply seen that he cannot be trusted, and rightly so."

The adviser contrasted that with Saudi Arabia’s relationships with "the Pakistanis and the Turkish brothers".

Saudi social media has also reflected opposition to Egypt's inclusion in the pact, with several accounts supportive of the kingdom’s leadership posting material suggesting Cairo was not wanted in the agreement.

The anonymous social media account @Columbuos, widely believed to belong to Saud al-Qahtani, a former senior aide to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is still considered a close advisor to the young royal, echoed this sentiment.

"The door of the alliance is not open to those who only want to address their problems and benefit from it without participating in the same secure mission for the region. Whoever wants to join must share the same common interests of the three countries," he said.

"The era of illusory entitlements, charity, and one-sided giving has passed, and the time of 'my fate alone' has ended, giving way to the phase of 'our single fate'," he added.

Despite this, all three sources stressed that the agreement did not necessarily close the door to Egypt joining in the future, but Riyadh’s position was that Cairo should remain on the outside for now.

item.description:
Tucker Carlson says Israel pushed him to report false allegations against Hunter Biden

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 20:30
Former US president's son says a 'Netanyahu operation centre' was involved in disseminating alleged drug and sex leaks
US President Joe Biden (L) and son Hunter step out of a bookstore while shopping in Nantucket, Massachusetts, on 29 November 2024 (Mandel Ngan/AFP)
Off

Conservative US commentator Tucker Carlson said Israeli "agents" close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed him to falsely report that Hunter Biden’s leaked laptop material showed him abusing minors.

"The claim that there was material involving the abuse of minors on the computer came from the Israelis," Carlson said in an interview aired on Monday with Hunter, former US President Joe Biden's son. "I'm just telling you that they came to me with it, and that's how I know it.”

Carlson’s claim dates back to 2020 when he was a presenter at the right-wing cable news network Fox and pushed allegations that Hunter was involved in corrupt business dealings with Ukraine when his father was vice president.

The younger Biden’s laptop story emerged in the weeks before the 2020 US election, which President Biden went on to win against President Donald Trump.

The story started with John Paul Mac Isaac, a computer repair shop owner in Wilmington, Delaware, who said Hunter left a damaged Apple computer and an external hard drive at his shop in April 2019. The FBI obtained possession of the laptop in December 2019.

In October 2020, The New York Post reported on emails contained in the laptop that detailed the younger Biden’s business dealings with Burisma, a Ukrainian energy company whose board Hunter sat on.

Other personal information obtained from the laptop and hard drive included videos of Hunter smoking crack, having sex and soliciting female prostitutes. Photos and videos of Hunter's drug- and alcohol fuelled rendezvous with prostitutes circled online during the early years of his father's presidency and were reported on regularly by Fox and The New York Post.

Carlson said that the false allegation about abuse of minors was a product of Israel’s misinformation campaign and was falsely attributed by former US intelligence officials to Russian propaganda.

Tucker Carlson interrogated in Israel, has passport seized after interviewing US ambassador
Read More »

“They (Israel) were behind it," Carlson said. ”I felt like everybody in Washington knew it, but there was so much pressure not to criticise Israel in any way that they just said, 'It's the Russians, it's the Russians'.”

"Maybe the Russians had a hand in it, but it was the Israelis who were pushing that fact," Carlson said. ”Fact, I mean literally [pushing it] to me.”

There is no evidence that Hunter abused minors. The former US president's son has long acknowledged the videos, texts and photos showing him engaging in drug and sex acts. 

For his part, Carlson acknowledged not sharing the Israeli angle when he was covering the story for Fox News. 

Hunter said that he didn’t have confirmation of who was behind his laptop leak, but said several parties were behind the dissemination of the laptop's material, including Russians, domestic US opponents of his father, and a "Netanyahu operation centre, the Israeli side”.

Hunter joined Carlson in criticising Netanyahu.

"If pointing out that Benjamin Netanyahu is evil incarnate is antisemitic, then I don't know what to tell people anymore," Hunter said.

item.description:
US rights groups sue Trump administration over ICC sanctions

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 20:40
The president's targeting of the court has created legal risk for US-based human rights advocates
A man takes a photograph of the exterior of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the Netherlands on 28 March 2026 (John Thys/AFP)
Off

Four US-based rights groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday for its sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC).

In a statement, the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch, and the Open Society Institute called the sanctions "blatantly illegal". 

They said they are being forced "to curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of... First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act", given that anyone who appears to associate with ICC cases or officials could now face legal repercussions. 

Just days after he assumed power in late January 2025, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order to sanction the ICC over its investigations into top Israeli officials.

British barrister Karim Khan, who was the ICC's chief prosecutor, was the only person named as a sanctioned individual.  

He has since been removed through a member states' vote, albeit due to sexual assault allegations. Khan has denied them. 

The executive order followed a White House visit by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza since October 2023.

Netanyahu and his then defence minister, Yoav Gallant, were issued arrest warrants in November 2024, alongside three Hamas leaders, who have since been killed by Israel.

All non-US individuals and their family members who assist in ICC investigations of US citizens or allies fall under the sanctions order. Their assets are frozen, they cannot use the international banking system, and they cannot enter the US.

This is not the first lawsuit in response to US sanctions. 

In July, advocates for Palestinian rights in the US filed a lawsuit in a New York City federal court, seeking an injunction to stop the Trump administration's enforcement of sanctions against groups or individuals liaising with the ICC.

Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, as well as the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), said they felt compelled to immediately go to court after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in an opinion piece that the US was willing to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick". 

'No basis in fact'

The lawsuit insists that Trump's powers to sanction the ICC "are based on a pseudo national emergency that has no basis in fact", the groups said on Tuesday. 

ICC states decision on Karim Khan ‘inherently political’, says leading criminal law expert
Read More »

"The sanctions have stopped the four plaintiff organizations from continuing or undertaking activities like representing victims of war crimes as legal counsel, making legal and policy submissions to the ICC, and collaborating with the sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups to undertake litigation, coordinate advocacy campaigns, research human rights violations, or provide humanitarian aid," the statement said.

Last year the Trump administration also sanctioned several Palestinian human rights organisations, many of which receive legal and financial support from US experts and donors.

It also sanctioned officials in the Palestinian Authority (PA) and Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) over their work taking Israel to international courts.

According to the State Department, the unnamed officials were “undermining the prospects for peace”.

In his executive order, Trump said the ICC has "engaged in illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel".

The US and Israel are not state parties to the Rome Statute, which is the treaty that established the ICC in The Hague in 2002.

Both states have opposed the court’s investigation into alleged Israeli crimes in Palestine, launched by the ICC’s previous prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, in 2021. 

The court’s jurisdiction was based on the accession of the State of Palestine to the Rome Statute in 2015. That means the court can investigate Israeli individuals for crimes committed in occupied Palestine, which includes the Gaza Strip, the West Bank and East Jerusalem. 

But Israel and the US have challenged the court’s jurisdiction, saying they do not recognise Palestine as a state, and that Israel is best placed to investigate itself under the principle of complementarity as set out in Article 17 of the Rome Statute.

Trump’s order reiterated this view and described the arrest warrants as an abuse of power.

Dismantling the ICC

Last month, Rubio said the Trump administration is working to "dismantle the [International Criminal Court] brick by brick". 

“The ICC’s interfering with American military and law enforcement operations isn’t just only a grave overreach of its purported authorities. It would mean the death of the US as a sovereign and independent nation,” Rubio wrote in an opinion article published by The Wall Street Journal. 

He said that Americans likely don't know the names of the judges, prosecutors or presidents of the international court, and that they "shouldn't have to", while accusing the ICC of waging a war against the US.

'Textbook infringement': Palestine advocacy groups sue for immediate halt to Trump's ICC sanctions
Read More »

Rubio’s criticism noted "bipartisan" opposition to the court, which was founded in 2002 in response to genocides and atrocities in war zones such as Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

Rubio made no direct mention of the outstanding arrest warrant issued for Netanyahu and Gallant in his article.

The European Union warned earlier this year that Trump's order has the potential to seriously affect the ICC's work in all investigations, not just on Palestine.

The court is currently investigating alleged crimes in 16 situations, including Darfur, Ukraine, Venezuela, Afghanistan, and Myanmar. 

But also last month, the new Venezuelan government - effectively run by Rubio himself from afar - withdrew from the ICC.

In a post on X, the US State Department hailed the move as marking a "partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC".

It pointed to an investigation by the court into former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, who was abducted from the South American country during a US military assault in January 2026, saying it had produced "no result".

"The ICC has instead wasted its resources on investigating and charging persons from countries that have competent, independent judicial systems and which never submitted to the jurisdiction of the court," the statement read.

"This is blatant overreach, political bias and selective enforcement," it said, adding that the court is "neither credible, independent, nor legitimate".

item.description:
Israel and Venezuela restore diplomatic relations after years of severed ties

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 19:54
The rapprochement comes after the US has for months boasted of running Venezuela, following the capture of Maduro
Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez speaks during a press conference at the Generalisimo Francisco de Miranda Air Base in Caracas, on 2 July 2026 (Lucas Agauyo/AFP)
Off

Israel and Venezuela announced the restoration of official diplomatic relations after 17 years of severed ties in mutual statements published on Tuesday. 

The rapprochement comes under acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, who has realigned Venezuela towards the US since she took office in January, after the US abduction and imprisonment of then-President Nicolas Maduro.

US President Donald Trump has boasted of running Venezuela following the capture of Maduro.

In a statement posted on X, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said that the two countries had "agreed to establish a coordination mechanism that will enable the provision of consular services to citizens of both countries".

A similar statement was posted by Venezuela's foreign minister, Felix Plasencia Gonzalez. 

Venezuela had long been one of a slim list of non-Muslim majority states with no official relations with Israel.

The Bolivarian Republic first severed ties in 2009 under leftist President Hugo Chavez in response to mass civilian casualties during Israel's first major war on Gaza, known in Israel as Operation Cast Lead. 

Official relations between the two countries remained frozen for decades after Chavez was succeeded by Maduro, who instead deepened Venezuela's diplomatic ties with both the Palestinian Authority and Iran.

A wave in Latin America

Tuesday's statement comes after months of unofficial ties between the two states since Maduro's abduction by the US.

In February, Bloomberg reported that Venezuelan oil had been shipped to Israel for the first time in decades, prompting denials from Venezuela's minister of information. 

Why is Latin America becoming a breeding ground for 'fanatics of Israel'?
Read More »

Israel later provided Venezuela with relief and assistance after a devastating double earthquake hit the country in June, killing over 6,000. 

Statements from both Israel and Venezuela each touted the "importance of the connection between the State of Israel and the Jewish community of Venezuela". There are around 6,000 Jews in Venezuela, according to the World Jewish Congress. 

Israel has welcomed a wave of support from Latin American states in recent months amid the election of several right-wing leaders across the continent, and in spite of Israel's genocide in Gaza, where over 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. 

Venezuela's announcement comes the same day as neighbouring Colombia recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, territory that is widely regarded as part of Syria under international law. 

Colombia's new far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced plans to normalise relations with Israel and open a controversial embassy in Jerusalem last month. 

Last week, the administration of Honduras' right-wing president, Nasry Asfura Zablah, also announced it had returned its ambassador to Israel, having withdrawn the representation amid the genocide in Gaza.

Zablah, along with the pro-Israel Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, is of Palestinian descent.
